item.title: State media new footage offers rare, multi-angle look at GJ-11 drone, revealing design details behind its stealth
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 21:24:00
The GJ-11 stealth drone Photo: Screenshot from CCTV News military channel CCTV News military channel released new footage on Monday offering a close-up, multi-angle look at the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force's GJ-11 stealth drone. It also revealed that two of the Air Force's first batch of self-trained female drone operators scored a first-round hit during the GJ-11's first live-fire strike mission. A military affairs expert explained how the design features shown in the video contribute to its stealth performance, and said the model has likely achieved combat and support capability, with technical maturity sufficiently assured. The GJ-11, codenamed "Xuanlong," is a domestically developed tailless flying-wing drone. The footage showed the GJ-11 up close, with details including its air intake, exhaust nozzle, landing gear and internal weapons bay doors revealing its high-stealth characteristics. According to CCTV, the GJ-11 has an air intake on top of its fuselage, a flattened tail section, and all weapons carried internally in a belly weapons bay that can accommodate a variety of air-to-surface munitions. It offers strong stealth, long endurance and high strike accuracy, and can carry out missions including air strikes and suppression of enemy air defense (SEAD). Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Monday that the multi-angle display makes the GJ-11's distinctive stealth design clearer. Its dorsal air intake is a design that enhances stealth, and its exhaust nozzle has also been treated for stealth, further improving survivability and enabling stealth-based penetration. It also uses radar-absorbing coatings to further reduce its radar cross-section. The CCTV military channel also revealed on Monday that two post-95s drone operators Shi Xiaoran and Fu Ting are among the first batch of female drone operators trained independently by the PLA Air Force. From newcomers to skilled operators, they completed their conversion training in just five months. In the GJ-11's first live-fire strike mission, Shi and Fu worked closely with their comrades and scored a first-round hit. A close-up look at the landing gear and internal weapons bay doors of the GJ-11 stealth drone Photo: Screenshot from CCTV News military channel CCTV said that the GJ-11 is a pioneer and a pathfinder. In future operations, striking ground targets will be a high-risk mission, and unmanned attack aircraft can reduce losses of personnel and weapons platforms. It will become an important partner and the most effective loyal wingman for main combat aircraft. Drone operators control the entire flight from inside a command cabin, issuing various instructions to manage the aircraft's attitude amid rapidly changing conditions. Their combat-oriented training in the cabin, tailored to mission needs, typically runs more than six hours per session, sometimes counted in days. The cabin is designed for mobile deployment: if a mission requires it, the entire cabin can be loaded directly onto a transport aircraft and sent straight to the front line, reported CCTV. "I found that drone iteration is beyond imagination. Many scenarios that appeared in sci-fi films are already being tried in real-world applications. In future battlefields, what matters more is a smart brain's perception of the battlefield situation and precise control of equipment. None of this has anything to do with gender, only with proficiency and hours of operation," Shi was quoted by CCTV as saying. The GJ-11 stealth attack drone was first unveiled at China's National Day military parade held in Beijing in 2019. It later made its appearance at China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition (also known as Airshow China) in Zhuhai, South China's Guangdong Province, in 2021. On this occasion, the GJ-11 opened its two belly weapons bays, each holding several precision-guided bombs, Global Times reporters observed at the scene. In November 2025, the PLA Air Force released a short film marking its 76th anniversary, revealing that the GJ-11 had entered service. The appearance marked the Air Force's official entry into a new model of manned-unmanned cooperative operations, said CCTV. The short film also showed for the first time an aerial formation composed of the GJ-11 stealth drone, the J-20 stealth fighter and the J-16D electronic warfare aircraft. Song called it a perfect combination for breaking through enemy defenses. A close-up look at the exhaust nozzle of the GJ-11 stealth drone Photo: Screenshot from CCTV News military channel Song supposed that the GJ-11 had undergone extensive testing before being fielded and forming aerial formations with the J-20 and J-16D, all core tests of its performance. He noted that the GJ-21, recently showcased alongside the Type 076 amphibious assault ship Sichuan, is in fact a carrier-based variant improved on the GJ-11. The GJ-11, as its predecessor, has likely achieved combat and support capability with sufficient technical maturity. The shift from an Air Force model to a Navy variant also shows the Air Force version's technical foundation is already mature, the expert said. With the 16th Airshow China approaching, military commentator Zhang Xuefeng said this year's show is expected to feature new drones. Whether the GJ-11 will appear and whether it can perform formation flights with other fighters are both worth watching. The GJ-11 is not the only advanced drone China has developed. At the V-Day military parade in Beijing on September 3, 2025, China for the first time displayed multiple types of wingman drones and air superiority drones. Military affairs experts told the Global Times that some of the UAVs showcased at the parade not only have new appearances, but also embody new concepts, which could overturn the existing air combat scenarios and profoundly change the future of air combat.

item.title: New BCI and neuromodulation technologies help military pilots combat mental fatigue, enhance performance
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 21:23:00
Photo: Screenshot from CCTV From brain-computer interfaces (BCI) and neuromodulation to advanced flight training technologies, an aerospace medicine summit hosted by the Air Force Medical University over the weekend in Xi’an, Northwest China’s Shaanxi Province, showcased the latest advances in aerospace medicine, flight training, and aeromedical rescue, China Central Television (CCTV) reported on Sunday. More than 1,000 experts and scholars from across China, including the military, gathered to discuss key challenges and cutting-edge developments with the aim of advancing high-quality scientific and technological innovation in aerospace medicine, according to CCTV. At this year's forum, a key topic of discussion was the application of BCI and neuromodulation technologies to strengthen aircrew members' physical and psychological resilience and sustained combat effectiveness under high-intensity missions. Experts discussed ways to protect aircrew from extreme physical and psychological stress, improve personnel selection and training, and leverage digital intelligence to enhance aviation capabilities. Yang Liu of the Air Force Medical University said pilots undergo training using breathing exercises and biofeedback before missions. Between missions or afterward, brief and safe transcranial microcurrent stimulation can be used to modulate brain regions associated with cognitive functions, helping pilots quickly alleviate mental fatigue. In addition, efficient personnel selection and training, as well as the integration of digital intelligence technologies, were among the key topics discussed at the forum. The forum also highlighted advanced flight training technologies, including a spatial disorientation simulator that recreates illusions encountered during night flights and when flying through clouds. The immersive system helps pilots maintain spatial awareness and better control their aircraft, enhancing flight safety. For example, when some pilots conduct training exercises in the deserts of northwest China, both the night sky and the ground can be completely dark due to the absence of artificial lighting. Pilots may experience spatial disorientation, mistaking the ground for the sky and vice versa, posing serious safety risks. Specialized ground-based simulators recreate realistic flying environments to help pilots recognize and respond to such illusions effectively. The forum also featured innovations in cognitive computing and non-invasive BCI aimed at enhancing aircrew operational capabilities, including an attention assessment and training system. The system uses real-time eye-tracking and physiological data to monitor pilots' attention distribution, cognitive workload and stress levels in complex environments. Models based on expert knowledge automatically score performance, helping trainees identify weaknesses and undertake targeted training, driving a shift in cognitive skills training from experience-based instruction to data-driven training supported by digital technologies. In addition, emerging forms of information-driven, intelligent and unmanned warfare are changing combat injury patterns and casualty evacuation conditions, creating new challenges for aeromedical rescue and rapid treatment. Wang Jianqi of the Air Force Medical University said researchers had developed the Chinese military's first casualty-search drone. They had also made advances in using drones to inject emergency medication into injured personnel at distant locations, buying time for treatment. Advances in unmanned technologies are making unmanned equipment an increasingly important part of aeromedical rescue, helping overcome the limitations of traditional rescue operations. Global Times

item.title: Unitree's first consumer-grade robotic dog priced at 43,900 yuan, draws 1,000 orders on debut
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 21:21:00
A robotic dog interacts with visitors at the Unitree booth at the Shanghai National Exhibition Center in Shanghai, on November 5, 2026, during the first day of the 9th CIIE. Photo: VCG Chatting, playing cute, and even dancing - Chinese leading robotics maker Unitree Robotics and Hong Kong-listed intellectual property (IP) operator Star Plus Legend Holdings unveiled a consumer-grade robotic dog priced at 43,900 yuan ($6,150) at the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai. As Unitree's first consumer-grade collectible robotic dog, it secured an order for 1,000 units on launch day, the Global Times learned from Unitree Robotics on Monday. Named UNI-DOGGIE, the robotic dog made its global debut at the expo. It combines robotics technology with celebrity-related IP and trendy toy design. The product is positioned as a collectible for the consumer market and is Unitree's first robotic dog designed specifically for this market, according to the companies. Weighing about 19 kilograms, UNI-DOGGIE is equipped with 12 precision aluminum-alloy joint motors. It has a maximum movement speed of 2 meters per second, can step over obstacles up to 16 centimeters high and can climb slopes with inclinations of up to 40 degrees, according to Star Plus Legend Holdings. The robot can perform movements including running, jumping, walking on its front legs, performing lion-dance moves and dancing. It is also equipped with a nose-mounted camera for taking photos and videos, and supports leash-free automatic following. Users can remotely control the robot via a mobile app over 4G networks, while its software also supports over-the-air updates, according to the company. The product is designed for a range of scenarios, including home companionship, outdoor activities, trendy toy gatherings, commercial performances and parent-child interaction. Its combination of mobility, interactive functions and collectible positioning reflects an effort to bring quadruped robots into consumer-oriented settings beyond industrial and research applications. In the robotics sector, Star Plus Legend Holdings said on its official website that it is working with Unitree Robotics to develop consumer-oriented IP robots, including quadruped robotic pets and humanoid robots for entertainment and performance scenarios. The two companies have established a joint venture responsible for the development and exclusive operation of related products. The cooperation between the two companies comes as Chinese humanoid robots and other robotic technologies have made significant progress and key breakthroughs in mobility and operational efficiency in recent years, marking rapid technological advancement. Data from China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology shows that the revenue of industrial enterprises above designated size in China's robotics sector exceeded 300 billion yuan in 2025, with an average annual growth rate of more than 20 percent in the past five years. China has become the world's most active market for robotics innovation and application. A report by California-based research firm Smart Analytics Global indicates that global humanoid robot shipments totaled approximately 19,100 units in the first half of 2026, with Chinese-made units accounting for more than 97 percent of the total, the Xinhua News Agency reported in August. Global Times

item.title: China appreciates Papua New Guinea's decision to close 'Taipei Economic Office,' stands ready to increase LNG imports: FM
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 20:07:00
Photo: Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun China appreciates Papua New Guinea's decision to close the "Taipei Economic Office," saying the move reaffirmed broad international support for the one-China principle, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday. Guo made the remark when asked to comment at the regular press conference that Taiwan's so-called "foreign affairs office" announced on November 6 the closure of the "Taipei Economic Office" in Port Moresby, and that "no new spot contracts" for the purchases of liquefied natural gas will be signed with Papua New Guinea. Taiwan also said that Papua New Guinea renewed its unilateral demands for personnel of the "office" to leave the country within a specified timeframe and for the "office" to be shut down. The decision by the government of Papua New Guinea to close the "Taipei Economic Office" in Papua New Guinea once again shows that upholding the one-China principle is where international public opinion trends and the arc of history bends, Guo said, emphasizing that China appreciates this and will continue working with Papua New Guinea to firmly support each other's core interests and major concerns. Guo further noted that China stands ready to increase imports of liquefied natural gas from Papua New Guinea, deepen cooperation in economy and trade and other areas, and add new dimensions to our comprehensive strategic partnership. Global Times

item.title: From salmon to kiwifruit, how China's logistics puts 'global freshness' on Chinese tables
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 19:58:00
People queue up to buy Zespri kiwifruit at the brand's booth at the CIIE in Shanghai on November 9, 2026. Photo: Tu Lei/Global Times Of all the halls at the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) held in Shanghai, the food and agricultural products halls are always the busiest. Fruits from all over the world are laid out in tidy rows, each display drawing crowds of visitors who line up for a taste, packed shoulder to shoulder. The smell of grilled meat hangs in the air, mingling with the smell of coffee — it feels less like an exhibition hall than a fairground. Behind that aroma is a supply chain few visitors see — one that moves fresh food from farm and fishing boat to the expo floor with barely a pause. At the CIIE, China Eastern Airlines' logistics subsidiary once again served up a "gourmet deal," signing a salmon supply agreement with Denmark's Skagen Salmon. During this November, China Eastern will open a cargo route linking Shanghai with Copenhagen, adding another efficient air artery between China and northern Europe. Salmon is not alone. From kiwifruit to blueberries and avocados, this responsiveness in China's logistics rests on steadily expanding cargo flying routes and improving services — explaining why more foreign goods reach Chinese tables faster and with greater ease. Fresh Atlantic salmon on display at a CIIE booth in Shanghai on November 9, 2026 Photo: Tu Lei/Global Times Higher efficiency With China's demand for imported salmon rising, the cold chain logistics firm under China Eastern went looking for suppliers in Denmark, where its route capacity could meet premium European supply. Talks with Skagen Salmon found alignment on origin resources, air freight and Chinese market channels, and the CIIE provided the platform that sealed the partnership, according to the information China Eastern shared with the Global Times. Keeping a "fresh" chain that spans thousands of miles running smoothly would take more than speed in the air: it depends on refined, digitally enabled quality control. The cold chain logistics firm worked closely with Skagen to clear each bottleneck in turn, and has built a one-stop cross-border supply chain solution. The chain now runs without a break: origin transport, port customs clearance, cold storage and end-to-end temperature tracking, then processing at the company's fresh-food hubs, and final delivery to supermarkets and livestream e-commerce channels, China Eastern said. For example, the logistics firm has built its own in-pack temperature logger, which tracks conditions along the entire journey and yields a full temperature curve — giving the company a record to trace where any anomaly began. And, at the Zespri booth at CIIE, kiwifruit from New Zealand sat in neat, orderly rows. Michael Jiang, president of Zespri China and APAC South, told the Global Times that, on March 17, the Panama-flagged vessel Kowhai, carrying more than 4,750 tons of the new-season fruit, sailed from New Zealand's Port of Tauranga and arrived in Shanghai 12 days later. The first batch of more than 3,000 boxes arrived at an agricultural products trading center in Shanghai on April 2 and sold out on its first day on the market. "We will keep innovating, sustain our steadfast partnerships in China, and keep Zespri at the forefront of the kiwifruit category here," Jiang said. Over the past nine years, Zespri has both witnessed and benefited from China's widening opening-up. For the 2026/27 season, the company expects global sales of 260 million standard retail trays and revenue of NZ$6.3 billion ($3.5 billion). Sales in China are projected to reach NZ$1.4 billion, with an annual volume of more than 1.5 billion kiwifruit reaching 34.37 million Chinese households. Its retail footprint has expanded from 35 Chinese cities in 2019 to 82 cities in 2026, according to the data the company shared with the Global Times. Expanding routes Widening routes are not about a single corridor or a single market. New cargo services, direct sailings and intermediate feeder networks are shortening the distance between overseas producers and Chinese consumers — and the change is reaching markets well beyond Asia. Wang Bin, general manager of COSCO SHIPPING Ports Chancay Peru, told the Global Times on Sunday that freight volumes have grown very rapidly in the two years since Chancay Port began operations in November 2024. The company's overall operating capacity at the port is 1 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), and this year's throughput is expected to approach half that capacity. It has opened five feeder routes serving neighboring countries, consolidating cargo from around South America at Chancay for shipment to China and other destinations in the Asia-Pacific. Chancay Port, in operation since November 2024, is one of China's most representative BRI investment projects in South America. It has established a direct shipping corridor linking China with South America's west coast, helping bring products such as avocados and blueberries from Peru to China. The direct sailing time from Chancay to Shanghai has been cut to just 23 days now, reducing logistics costs by more than 20 percent. From January to September of this year, 62 percent of Peru's agricultural exports to China were shipped via the Chancay Port, generating sales of about $210 million. The port provides an efficient route for Peruvian specialty products to access the Chinese market, according to the official website of the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council (SASAC). More and more overseas agricultural products are using the CIIE as a platform and China's mature cross-border cold chain network to travel from fishing boats, farms and ranches straight to exhibition booths and supermarket shelves — a vivid illustration of how China's logistics services have become so cost-efficient. For overseas exporters behind those shipments, the CIIE is less a once-a-year showcase than a standing invitation from 1.4-billion-consumer giant market: ship your fine goods to China.

item.title: Inner Mongolia International Communication Center uses digital storytelling to boost global visibility
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 13:38:00
The Inner Mongolia International Communication Center is unveiled on November 8, 2026. Photo: Courtesy of IMICC The Inner Mongolia International Communication Center (IMICC) was unveiled in Hohhot, North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region on Sunday, according to a press release sent to the Global Times by the center. The establish of IMICC marks the latest effort of Inner Mongolia to promote cultural exchange and mutual understanding through international communication. IMICC is committed to building an international platform reaching out to neighboring countries and engaging audiences around the world. It will tell stories of China in the new era, particularly the new grassland Silk Road, and let the world see a vibrant Inner Mongolia, per the center. IMICC traces its roots back more than 30 years, originating from a Mongolian-language magazine Solonggo launched in 1993. Based on the Solonggo media outlets, the new IMICC marks a further step forward in upgrading the platform, with new multi-lingual websites in Chinese, English and Russian, and official WeChat accounts and channels. It has also launched overseas social media accounts in English, Russian and Slavic languages. These efforts develop a multi-channel, multi-dimensional international communication network to tell stories of China and Inner Mongolia, said the center. IMICC is dedicated to grounding national narratives in relatable, everyday stories from the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Drawing on the region's high-quality development practices, it seeks out compelling stories and distinctive communication highlights, using small yet meaningful perspectives - a landscape that reflects the broader picture, an object that embodies cultural heritage, or an individual event that offers a glimpse of the bigger picture - to showcase the region's magnificent natural scenery, rich cultural heritage and remarkable achievements in advancing Chinese modernization. Through these efforts, the center aims to enhance Inner Mongolia's visibility and influence on the international stage, helping the world gain a better understanding of China and the region. Guided by the principles of people-centered storytelling, video-based presentation and digital-first communication, it has launched a series of internationally oriented, internet-savvy and youth-friendly communication products, including Learning Chinese, I'm Happy in Inner Mongolia and Colorful Inner Mongolia. These products take various forms, including news reports, short videos, documentaries, exclusive interviews, livestreams and commentaries.

item.title: Filipinos lining up for Chinese visas, yet anti-China politicians in Manila pretend to be asleep
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 11:29:00
Filipinos line up to apply for Chinese visas. Photo: Screenshot of a post published by Philippine media outlet Daily Tribune on Facebook Several Filipino netizens recently shared photos on social media showing long lines at the visa application service center of the Chinese Embassy in Manila. One netizen, recounting their experience of applying for a Chinese visa, said there were more than 300 people ahead of them when they submitted their application. Despite arriving as soon as the visa office opened, they had to wait a full five hours to complete the process. In the photos, even the stairways leading to the visa office were packed with people. Despite the long wait, the anticipation and excitement on their faces were unmistakable. According to Philippine media reports, nearly 235,000 Filipino tourists traveled to China between January and September this year, a year-on-year surge of approximately 51 percent, even as the total number of outbound travelers from the Philippines increased by just 7.16 percent. The growth is still accelerating. The Chinese Embassy in the Philippines has had to advise visa applicants to avoid peak hours, consider applying in groups and plan their applications accordingly. After seeing the photos, many netizens expressed surprise at just how many Filipinos wanted to visit China. Some attributed China's growing appeal as a travel destination to factors such as travel vloggers sharing their experiences and highly affordable travel packages. So far, Philippine officials, especially those clowns who frequently stir up trouble for China-Philippines relations, have continued to bury their heads in the sand, offering no response to this trending topic on Philippine social media. They are precisely the ones who should come forward and explain themselves. For a long time, these politicians have repeatedly stirred up trouble in the South China Sea while clinging to external powers for support. At the same time, they have relentlessly hyped up the so-called "China threat" in domestic public discourse, portraying China as a place fraught with traps and dangers at every turn. But here is the question: If China really is such a "threat," why are more and more Filipinos willing to stand in line for hours to visit? This demonstrates just how completely disconnected from reality these politicians' carefully crafted narratives have become. In fact, for these politicians, being "anti-China" is merely a political performance. While publicly shouting anti-China slogans, they have also sought to profit from the Chinese market, trying to have it both ways. Some of them, after being hit with tough Chinese sanctions, have seen their avenues for personal gain completely cut off. As a result, they have become increasingly hysterical, stepping up their efforts to provoke confrontation at every opportunity. Some Filipinos have also complained on social media that these politicians, who criticize China day in and day out, actually want to send their own family members there. This exposes their selfish motives more clearly than any public statement ever could. The long lines on those stairways offer a glimpse into what ordinary Filipinos really think. Those anti-China political performances are like soap bubbles: They do not even need to be pricked to burst. They will collapse on their own.

item.title: Global South delegates seek stronger voice at World Media Summit in Beijing
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09 09:33:00
A guest attending the 7th World Media Summit views dexterous robotic hands at the Zhongguancun Exhibition Center in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 6, 2026. (Xinhua/Mao Zhu) Senior media professionals from the Global South have called for closer cooperation at the 7th World Media Summit in Beijing to give their countries a stronger voice in global coverage as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the industry. Co-organized by Xinhua News Agency and the Beijing municipal government, this year's summit runs from Nov. 5 to 9. It has drawn nearly 500 representatives of media outlets, think tanks and government bodies from 112 countries and regions, as well as the United Nations and other international organizations. Initiated in 2009, the World Media Summit has become a major platform for exchange and cooperation among media leaders and professionals across regions and language communities. "What is important about the summit is that it brings media outlets from around the world and gives us a forum to discuss the future of our industry," said Kenedid Ibrahim Houssein, director of publication of La Nation in Djibouti, who is attending the summit for the first time. "We hope to further develop partnership with China on information sharing based on this platform," he added. Ghislain Ruffin Etoughet Nzuet, chairman of the board of directors at Gabon Broadcasting Corporation, said the World Media Summit provides a platform for African countries to tell their own stories and speak for themselves. "Africa has a long tradition and a long history, yet very little is known about us," Nzuet said, adding that cooperation with partners around the world, particularly China, could help bring African perspectives into global discussions. Agnes Kalekye Nguna, managing director and CEO of Kenya Broadcasting Corporation, stressed the importance of dialogue among civilizations on an equal footing. She called for more initiatives to expand exchanges and deepen media cooperation between Africa and China, saying a partnership that benefits both sides could inspire similar efforts elsewhere in the Global South and beyond. Under this year's theme, "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action," delegates are also discussing how Global South countries could work together to help their media organizations adapt as AI use expands across the industry. "How do we ensure smaller nations have a meaningful voice in shaping the future of AI?" asked Aminath Namza, chairperson of Public Service Media in the Maldives, during discussions at the summit. She said many AI models are trained on data drawn mainly from societies with a greater digital presence, and therefore may not be able to fully reflect the languages, cultures and realities of smaller nations. "International cooperation must therefore ensure that developing countries and small island states can contribute not only to AI's development, but also to the principles governing it," she said. On Saturday, the 7th World Media Summit released the Global Media Initiative for the Joint Development of AI Application Standards. Launched by Xinhua, the initiative brings together major media outlets and other professional organizations to safeguard the authenticity of information, protect data security, and uphold media ethics, thereby maintaining public trust in the media. Under this initiative, participants plan to work together for about two years to develop a set of standards that address different media uses of AI and are validated by media outlets. Najeh Missaoui, director general and CEO of Tunis Afrique Presse, one of the first participants, regards the initiative as a major step forward. "It takes us from talking about AI to taking joint action and setting rules." "For us at Tunis Afrique Presse, this plan ensures that the Global South will have a hand in shaping the rules for AI, rather than simply consuming technology developed by others," he said. "We hope the initiative will become a practical avenue for cooperation, sharing expertise and building capacity, and media organizations of different sizes and with different resources can apply the standards," said Mohammed Alyami, director general of the Union of News Agencies of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, which is also among the first participants, in an interview with Xinhua. Wong Chun Wai, chairman of the Malaysian National News Agency (Bernama), said that, instead of access to basic AI tools, media organizations need to invest in advanced tools and train staff to use them effectively. He called on Global South countries to work together more closely in the changing media landscape and ensure that media organizations worldwide can share in the benefits of AI. Adopted at the summit on Saturday, the 7th World Media Summit Beijing Consensus calls for joint efforts to advance the transformation and development of the global media industry in the AI era. It commits to advancing the inclusive and responsible application of AI in the media sector so that advances in AI benefit media organizations at all stages of development and in every country. "The future of global communication must be intelligent, but above all, inclusive," said Viasen Soobramoney, CEO of South Africa's Independent Media IOL and the African News Agency, during the summit. Soobramoney called for transparent, accountable and inclusive global AI governance to help prevent the technology from reinforcing inequalities that have long affected many Global South countries. Africa and China could deepen cooperation in AI-assisted translation, multimedia production, journalist training, content verification and the exchange of technical expertise, he said. Abdul Hakim, president director of Indonesia's Antara News Agency, suggested closer cooperation on information sharing and verification, more exchanges on responsible AI use and newsroom innovation, and better coordination in reporting on global challenges. "No country, no community, and no voice should be left behind," he said. "This is why international cooperation matters so much."

item.title: 'US data, computing in China' is more than just a tongue-in-cheek phrase: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08 23:05:00
AI Photo: VCG In the era of AI, the US is tested not only on its innovative capacity but also on its ability to coordinate public interests and objectively recognize the strengths of other countries. The simple insight from "US data, computing in China" lies in the need for open perspectives and pragmatic cooperation in development. Could North American tech companies choose to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers in China? Following the conclusion of the US midterm elections, the debate surrounding AI data centers has moved further onto the US public policy agenda. Against this backdrop, a tongue-in-cheek phrase - "US data, computing in China" - has suddenly gained traction online. The idea behind it is that if the construction of data centers in the US faces obstacles, American tech companies may have little choice but to build more offshore data centers. China is one of the few economies in the world with the equipment supply chains and power infrastructure needed to support such facilities. In theory, "US data, computing in China" could therefore represent a solution for the optimal allocation of resources. The emergence of this online quip reflects a real problem: the bottlenecks facing the expansion of AI computing capacity in the US. As a global AI powerhouse, the US is experiencing a surge in demand for computing power, yet upgrades to its power grid infrastructure are lagging significantly behind. Large-scale computing clusters face lengthy waits for grid connection approvals. In addition, following the midterm elections, a growing number of measures restricting data center development may be passed, casting considerable uncertainty over whether new data center projects can move forward. Meanwhile, data centers in the US are expensive and time-consuming to build. Despite continued capital investment, computing capacity is being delivered at a sluggish pace, failing to keep up with the rapid evolution of AI models and customer demand. The gap between supply and demand continues to widen. China, by contrast, offers lower energy costs, more stable power supplies and a more comprehensive supporting industrial ecosystem. More importantly, China has the capacity to coordinate industrial development with infrastructure construction. Initiatives such as the "East Data, West Computing" project and the development of a nationwide integrated computing network emphasize regional coordination, the integration of computing power and electricity, and security safeguards. Together, they provide an institutional framework and safeguard for matching computing demand with available resources. China's ability to execute large-scale engineering projects, its supporting infrastructure and its capacity for long-term planning all have the potential to reduce construction coordination costs. Some estimates suggest that data center projects in the US generally take more than three years to complete, while comparable 100-megawatt projects in China can now be delivered in about 12 months. Construction costs per megawatt are estimated to be around $8 million to $12 million in the US, compared with approximately $5.5 million to $6.5 million in China. In this sense, "US data, computing in China" could be a viable avenue for cooperation. The US has accumulated considerable strengths in frontier research and software ecosystems, while China excels in various aspects, including industrial supply chains, engineering and construction capabilities, the number of engineers, and the availability of diverse application scenarios. If the two countries can leverage these complementary strengths in appropriate areas, they could help reduce the overall costs of AI development, ease resource constraints and extend the benefits of technological progress to a broader segment of society. Comparative advantages can be jointly created and continuously enhanced through cooperation. Of course, such cooperation would require clearly defined boundaries. Data involving national security, personal privacy and critical infrastructure should be subject to strict safeguards. Cross-border computing services would also need to take into account network latency, data transmission costs, intellectual property rights and regulatory compliance requirements, among other factors. However, why does this seemingly reasonable solution become a subject of ridicule in reality? The reason is obvious: Washington's political thinking of abusing the concept of security in relation to technology issues. For some time now, the US has weaponized digital elements such as computing power, chips, and data to a high degree. The export control list keeps getting longer, restrictions on advanced chips to China are tightening layer by layer, and investment review mechanisms are increasingly fortified. Not to mention, relocating the US computing power center to China, even specific projects that US and Chinese companies currently want to collaborate on, could easily be thrust under the political microscope and subjected to intense scrutiny amid the increasingly toxic political climate in the US. From a certain perspective, "US data, computing in China" is less about offering advice to American companies and more about netizens mocking Washington's "decoupling and disruption of industrial and supply chains" in the field of digital technology. Although "US data, computing in China" is far from reality, further extending the cooperation list in the AI field between China and the US is possible and necessary. The Chinese people's aspiration for a better life and the American people's desire to improve their lives and revitalize industries share a space of mutual interest. If "Make America Great Again" includes lowering living costs, increasing quality employment, and improving public facilities, then engaging in pragmatic cooperation with China can also be a viable option for achieving these goals. Mutual success should reflect tangible benefits that both peoples can perceive. At the same time, as two influential entities in the global AI field, it is also the shared responsibility of both countries to improve AI global governance and promote inclusive development. In the era of AI, the US is tested not only on its innovative capacity but also on its ability to coordinate public interests and objectively recognize the strengths of other countries. The simple insight from "US data, computing in China" lies in the need for open perspectives and pragmatic cooperation in development. As long as the US can shed its Cold War mentality and move toward China, adhering to a people-centered approach and developing AI for the positive and for good, there will still be opportunities to transform real pressures into momentum for common development, allowing AI to truly serve the progress of humanity. The world needs such cooperation.

item.title: GT Voice: China's cruise takeoff will create wider room for co-op
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08 21:54:00
Photo: VCG China's two domestically built large cruise ships were spotted berthing side by side at Wusongkou in Shanghai on Sunday, in what was reportedly their first such encounter. Adora Magic City , the country's first homegrown large cruise ship, was joined by the newly delivered Adora Flora City . Large cruise ships are among the most complex engineering undertakings in the global industrial system. The sight of the two vessels side by side in Shanghai captures a turning point for China's shipbuilding industry, from the breakthrough of building the first large cruise ship to the capacity for serial production. But for the international shipbuilding industry, there is more to this story. The gathering at Wusongkou is only the beginning. Adora Flora City will begin its inaugural season on November 22. The ship is entering a market with growing consumer demand. China has become one of the fastest-growing cruise markets in Asia and in the world. According to an industry report, the country handled 1.265 million cruise passenger trips in the first 11 months of 2025, up 27.8 percent year-on-year. China's advances in large cruise shipbuilding are set to intensify competition in the global shipbuilding industry. As Chinese shipyards continue to develop their technological capabilities, that competition is likely to become more pronounced. But that is only one side of the story. China's expanding cruise market is creating new commercial opportunities for international companies, even as Chinese shipbuilders become more competitive. China's progress in the industry is not only changing the competitive landscape but also expanding the market for the industry as a whole. Shipbuilding is an extraordinarily complex industry, underpinned by an extensive network of suppliers and supporting businesses. Large cruise ships take that complexity to another level. Adora Flora City , for instance, reportedly incorporates more than 25 million components, drawing on a network of 1,500 suppliers from China and abroad. These figures offer a glimpse of the commercial ecosystem surrounding China's shipbuilding industry, linking shipyards with suppliers and businesses across the wider value chain in an intricate web of commercial relationships. Two developments are advancing China's shipbuilding industry: technological progress and the expanding consumer market. Both need to be seen in the context of the industry's extensive supply chain. As China's shipbuilding sector moves forward, so does the wider industrial ecosystem around it which will generate greater opportunities for Chinese and international companies alike. The scale of the Chinese market offers international companies more than one way to participate in its growth. They can compete with Chinese shipbuilders, while also finding opportunities to cooperate by supplying technologies, specialized equipment and services. As the industry develops, the growing industrial network is creating more commercial opportunities that extend well beyond shipyards. South Korea has maintained a strong position in high-value and high-tech shipbuilding, while Japan and some European countries retain strengths in specialized segments, including cruise ship construction. Such differences reflect the depth of expertise across the global shipbuilding industry. China's rapid progress has led some international observers to focus on the competitive pressure the global industry faces. But that perspective risks obscuring a parallel development: the scope for cooperation across the industry's supply chain is expanding alongside China's own capabilities. The more Chinese shipbuilding industry grows, the greater the potential for international companies to participate in that growth. That opportunity, however, will not be there for the taking. International suppliers will need to offer specialized equipment and advanced services that meet the increasingly sophisticated demands of Chinese shipbuilders and customers. The two luxury cruisers together at Wusongkou offer a snapshot of China's rapid manufacturing progress. For international companies, this signals a wider field of cooperation and opportunities. To bag these opportunities will require a competitive edge in technology and expertise.
